To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) semantic schemes are more expressive than syntactic ones, (b) semantic schemes are not yet as well understood as syntactic ones, but the gap is rapidly narrowing, (c) the main challenge in semantic representation research is to find the best trade-off between expressivity, complexity, and human interpretability, and (d) there is no single best representation scheme, and the choice of a particular scheme should depend on the task at hand and on the resources available

(a) semantic representations can be used as a bridge between the syntactic and the semantic levels of analysis, and that (b) semantic representations can also be used as a stand-alone analysis, in particular for tasks that do not require a complete analysis.

(a) semantic schemes are more expressive than syntactic schemes in that they can represent more complex semantic structures; (b) the expressivity gap is smaller than one may think at first glance, as syntactic schemes are able to represent a large number of complex semantic structures, too, and (c) semantic and syntactic schemes are complementary, and their integration in a single representation scheme would be desirable.
